newsitem.title: USA: US states back retroactive liability in Superfund.
newsitem.headline: US states back retroactive liability in Superfund.

text.p: The governer of the state with the most Superfund sites said Wednesday the federal hazardous waste cleanup law should be reformed to make sure that polluters, not developers, are held responsible.

At a House Transportation subcommittee hearing, New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman said under her state's program, parties that polluted are responsible for cleanup costs and future liabilities from the site, not developers who try to make the site useful again.
"We do not let responsible parties walk away from polluted sites, leaving the problem for taxpayers to solve," the Republican governor said of her state's program.

A number of Republicans in Congress have pushed for full or partial repeal of liability for parties who polluted before the Superfund law was enacted in 1980. That has been one of the major disagreements with the administration, which has insisted that those who dumped the dangerous waste should pay for the cleanup.
"The need is for reform of retroactive liability, not repeal of it," Water Resources subcommittee chairman Sherwood Boehlert, a New York Republican, said, .
The House Commerce and Transportation committees so far are not considering specific bills, while the Senate Environment Committee is working with a Republican plan.
The House subcommittee heard from officials from 10 states including New Jersey, who urged that the law provide more flexibilty to meet individual states' needs.

The officials also generally echoed Whitman in saying the law should keep the concept of "polluter pays," although several said municipal liability should be limited and very small parties to pollution may be exempted.

"While New York supports efforts to increase the fairness of the current CERCLA (Superfund) liability standard, we oppose the repeal of retroactive liability," John Cahill, acting commissions of New York state's Department of Environmental Conservation, said.
"Such a repeal likely would burden New York with millions of dollars of additional remedial expense which, given the many other deamnds on our fiscal resources, cannot be sustained," Cahill said.

In its program for sites that are under state authority, Michigan replaced strict liability for owners and operators of contaminated sites with a "causation standard" to make the actual polluters liable, Russel Harding, that state's Department of Environmental Quality director, said.
The state officials also called on Congress to delegate more responsibility and resources to states to undertake more of the cleanups themselves.
"It is time to turn this program over to states that demonstrate the expertise, capacity and willingness to do so," California's Secretary for Environmental Protection, James Strock, said.
